newsitem.title: PAKISTAN: Bhutto refiles plea to court after second refusal.
newsitem.headline: Bhutto refiles plea to court after second refusal.

text.p: Pakistan's ousted prime minister Benazir Bhutto refiled a petition against her sacking to the Supreme Court on Sunday, after twice before having it refused, her lawyer said.
"I have re-filed the same amended petition which the court had returned to us on Saturday," Bhutto's lawyer Aitzaz Ahsan told Reuters.
The court returned the first version of Bhutto's 42-page petition on Tuesday, saying it contained objectionable references to President Farooq Leghari and court chief justice Sajjad Ali Shah.

Her lawyers disputed this, but refiled the petition anyway on Thursday, omitting the offending passages with a separate letter to record Bhutto's disagreement with the court's refusal to accept her petition.

The court registrar returned the amended petition as well on Saturday saying the objections and disagreements raised in the letter were "frivolous and misconceived and cannot be allowed to be placed on the record."
The petition was refiled on Sunday minus the letter containing Bhutto's disagreement with the first court refusal, court sources said.

On Saturday, Ahsan had expressed surprise at the court registrar's advice to file an appeal, saying: "How can they force us to file an appeal when we don't want to and have actually deleted the portions objected to by the court."
He said on Sunday he expected the court to take up the petition within a couple of days.

Bhutto's petition challenges her November 5 dismissal by President Farooq Leghari on disputed charges of corruption and misrule and seeks a restoration of her government and the National Assembly (lower house of parliament), which was dissolved by the president.

The first petition contained blistering criticism of Leghari for dismissing the National Assembly and ousting Bhutto, whose three-year-old adminsitration was replaced by a caretaker government due to hold fresh elections on February 3.

Bhutto, campaigning for support on a train journey to the the Punjab province capital of Lahore on Sunday, told cheering crowds there that she sought justice "from Allah, and from the court of people".
Bhutto has said she will await the court's verdict before deciding whether to fight the February 3 general election.
Bhutto has accused Leghari of breaking his word not to use controversial presidential powers to dismiss governments.

Leghari, Bhutto's nominee for president after she took power in October 1993, has said she brought Pakistan to the brink of economic and social collapse, and was unable to distinguish between the state and the government.

The caretaker government, led by 80-year-old Meraj Khalid, has vowed to bring undisclosed charges against Bhutto and her husband, Asif Ali Zardari, who has been detained under a broad maintenance of public order law since his wife's overthrow.
